Pregnancy

Viral hepatitis in pregnancy: pregnancy loss, treatment and protecting the baby

Updated: November 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Hepatitis means inflammation of the liver. The viruses called hepatitis A, B, C, D and E do not have the same routes of spread, treatments or pregnancy risks. A hepatitis result does not by itself establish that a miscarriage will happen or explain a previous loss. It also should not be dismissed with a blanket promise that pregnancy is unaffected. The useful next step is to identify the virus, assess the pregnant person’s health and make a timely care and newborn-prevention plan.

Start with the type and the severity, not a general reassurance

A recent infection, a long-standing infection without advanced liver damage and an illness causing liver failure are different situations. The pregnancy stage, other infections, liver function and access to treatment also matter. Miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm birth and transmission to a baby are different outcomes; a number describing one cannot be used to predict another.

Hepatitis E deserves particular attention because symptomatic infection in pregnancy, especially later in pregnancy, can be severe for both the pregnant person and fetus. Hepatitis C has also been associated with preterm birth, reduced fetal growth and other complications in studies, although associations do not prove that the virus caused an individual outcome. Advanced liver disease adds risks whatever the original cause. Ask for an individual assessment rather than assuming either inevitable loss or no danger.

How the five viruses differ

Hepatitis A is usually spread through contaminated food or water or close contact involving the faecal–oral route. Hepatitis E can spread through contaminated water, and some types through raw or undercooked animal products. Hepatitis B and C are mainly concerns around infected blood; B can also spread through sexual body-fluid exposure. Both can pass from a pregnant person to a baby. Hepatitis D needs hepatitis B to replicate.

Acute means a recent, short-term infection; chronic means a persisting infection. A does not become chronic. B and C can, and D can persist with B. E is usually acute but can rarely become chronic, particularly in immunosuppressed people. Symptoms alone cannot reliably tell these viruses apart, and someone with B or C may feel well despite an infection requiring follow-up.

Hepatitis A: an acute infection, with prevention available

Hepatitis A usually resolves, but it can cause substantial illness and occasionally severe liver failure. It should not be labelled harmless because it does not become chronic. During pregnancy, vomiting, dehydration, jaundice or abdominal pain needs clinical assessment rather than a home diagnosis. Treatment usually supports hydration and recovery; severe illness may require hospital care.

A vaccine is available. In US CDC guidance, pregnancy vaccination is recommended when there is a risk of infection or a severe outcome and previous vaccination is absent; local recommendations and the exact product matter. After a possible exposure, contact a clinician promptly because vaccine or immunoglobulin may be appropriate and postexposure prevention is time-sensitive, generally within two weeks. Do not wait for symptoms or arrange injections yourself.

Hepatitis B: assess maternal infection and plan prevention

A positive hepatitis B surface antigen test, or HBsAg, indicates current infection. The team assesses whether infection is recent or chronic, checks liver health and usually measures HBV DNA to help assess the need for treatment and transmission prevention. Maternal viral activity and prevention measures matter; describing every exposure as a 90% transmission risk is inaccurate. The often-quoted figure of about 90% refers to chronic infection developing among infants who actually acquire HBV, not to every baby of a parent with HBV.

Some pregnant people need antiviral treatment for their own liver health, and some with high HBV DNA need it to reduce transmission. Specialist guidance commonly uses tenofovir, with timing determined by the clinical situation and local pathway. Do not start, switch or stop it yourself; stopping can require monitoring for a liver flare. Maternal treatment does not replace the baby’s birth protection. Caesarean birth is not recommended solely to prevent HBV transmission.

An HBV-exposed newborn needs an advance birth plan

Tell the maternity and newborn teams about a positive HBsAg result before delivery and make sure the result reaches the birth facility. Under US CDC guidance, a baby born to an HBsAg-positive person receives single-antigen hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immunoglobulin, or HBIG, within 12 hours of birth, at different injection sites. The vaccine helps build protection; HBIG supplies immediate antibodies. This applies even if the pregnant person received antivirals.

If the maternal result is unknown or undocumented, tell the team immediately: testing and newborn prevention must not wait for a routine appointment. The precise vaccine/HBIG pathway depends on available results, evidence of infection, birth weight and local guidance. If a planned dose was missed, contact the birth team urgently for a catch-up decision rather than assuming it is too late or waiting until the next scheduled vaccine. This is clinical prevention, not a home injection plan.

Finish the vaccine course and the baby’s tests

Birth protection is the start, not the whole course. In the US CDC pathway, exposed infants complete their vaccine series and have HBsAg and anti-HBs blood tests at 9–12 months, or one to two months after a delayed final dose, but not before nine months. Low birth weight can change the number and timing of doses. A well-looking baby still needs the planned tests; absence of symptoms does not prove that transmission was prevented.

Programmes differ. WHO recommends hepatitis B vaccination for all babies as soon as possible after birth, within 24 hours, followed by the course. England’s exposed-baby pathway uses a birth vaccine within 24 hours, HBIG for selected higher-risk babies, further vaccines and infection testing between one year and 18 months. These examples should not be combined into a new schedule. Ask your own team to document the exact birth medicines, later doses, test date and who will review the result, including if you move.

Hepatitis C: exposure does not mean infection

HCV can pass during pregnancy or birth when the pregnant person has current infection, shown by detectable HCV RNA. An antibody result alone may reflect an infection that has cleared. CDC estimates that roughly 6–7% of perinatally exposed infants acquire infection; this is a population estimate, not a personal prediction. Poorly controlled HIV coinfection raises risk, and effective HIV care is important.

There is no hepatitis C vaccine or routine birth immunoglobulin that prevents it. When feasible, cure HCV before pregnancy. During pregnancy, assess liver health and discuss treatment with a specialist: evidence for direct-acting antivirals is still limited, and they are not routinely recommended solely to prevent transmission. Ribavirin has specific pregnancy risks. Do not start or stop a medicine without advice, or infer that every antiviral has the same pregnancy or feeding profile.

HCV birth precautions, infant testing and feeding

A caesarean is not recommended solely to prevent HCV. Clinicians avoid unnecessary blood-exposing procedures such as internal fetal monitoring and early artificial membrane rupture when possible, while providing appropriate obstetric care. These precautions cannot guarantee prevention. Under the US CDC pathway, an exposed infant has an HCV RNA test at age 2–6 months, with age-based catch-up if missed. A detectable result needs specialist follow-up; local pathways can differ.

HCV is not documented to spread through breast milk or ordinary hugging and kissing. Cracked, damaged or bleeding nipples need a temporary feeding plan to avoid blood exposure; HIV coinfection and exact medicines need separate specialist advice. HBV infection also does not automatically prevent breastfeeding when the baby receives the appropriate birth prophylaxis. Keep parental liver follow-up and the child’s testing plan separate, even when both feel well.

Hepatitis D depends on B, but can make liver disease more serious

HDV cannot replicate without HBV. A person can acquire B and D together, or acquire D after already having chronic B; it is not restricted to people known to have B beforehand. D can accelerate serious liver disease. It is blood-borne and can also spread through sexual exposure; transmission around birth is possible but uncommon.

Preventing HBV through vaccination also prevents the B infection that allows D to establish itself in an uninfected person. It does not treat an existing B or D infection. If you have HBV, ask whether D testing is appropriate for your history and local guidance. A positive result needs specialist assessment of liver health, pregnancy and treatment options; do not transfer a B or C treatment plan to D yourself.

Hepatitis E can be particularly dangerous in pregnancy

HEV infection can cause acute liver failure, pregnancy loss and maternal death, with increased risk described particularly in the second and third trimesters. The risk varies with the setting and infection; a severe-outcome percentage from one group should not be presented as every person’s prediction. Symptomatic pregnant people need urgent assessment, and hospital care may be considered. HEV can also pass from a pregnant person to the baby. New jaundice or feeling unwell must not wait for a routine antenatal visit.

It is outdated to say that E never becomes chronic or that no vaccine exists. Chronic infection occurs rarely, especially with immunosuppression. An HEV vaccine is licensed in China and some other countries and has been used in outbreak responses, including campaigns involving pregnant women, but it is not a routinely available pregnancy vaccine everywhere. Ask local public-health or travel clinicians about actual availability and advice. Safe water, sanitation and properly cooked food remain important; do not self-treat hepatitis E with antivirals or liver remedies.

Testing and possible exposure need a timely conversation

Tell your maternity clinician about a previous hepatitis diagnosis, treatment, vaccine record, relevant travel, possible contaminated food or water, blood exposure and any HIV infection. Testing may include liver blood tests and virus-specific antibody, antigen or RNA tests. Routine antenatal screening does not necessarily test for all five viruses. The US recommends HBV and HCV screening in each pregnancy; available screening and follow-up vary internationally.

A needlestick, blood contact, sexual exposure or close contact with hepatitis A can call for prompt assessment even without symptoms. The clinician decides which tests, vaccination or other postexposure measures are appropriate and whether repeat testing is needed. A negative early result may not answer every recent exposure. Do not delay because you are worried about blame, and do not assume that a partner’s diagnosis establishes infection in you or the fetus.

Reduce exposure without replacing medical care

Use safe drinking water and follow local food-safety advice, including thorough cooking of meat and shellfish. Wash hands, especially after using the toilet and before preparing food. Do not share needles, injection equipment, razors or toothbrushes that may carry blood; use regulated services with appropriate infection control. Discuss sexual protection and whether close contacts need testing or vaccination, without stigma.

Avoid alcohol and ask your clinician or pharmacist before using nonprescription medicines, supplements or herbal products when liver disease is suspected or known. A product marketed as a liver detox is not a treatment for viral hepatitis. Keep prescribed treatment and monitoring under review rather than stopping independently. After delivery, continue the parent’s liver care as well as the baby’s vaccines and tests; preventing transmission does not mean the parent’s infection has been cured.

When the pregnant or postpartum person needs urgent help

Get urgent clinical advice if you think you have hepatitis, develop yellow eyes or skin, dark urine or pale stools, or feel unwell after a possible exposure. Contact maternity care urgently for pregnancy bleeding or pelvic pain, and immediately for reduced or changed usual fetal movements. Do not assume pain, jaundice, itching or vomiting is just a known hepatitis infection; other pregnancy conditions can need treatment.

Use emergency services for severe, worsening or movement/touch-provoked pelvic pain, or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, passing out, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or sudden confusion. Pregnancy bleeding with severe abdominal pain, shoulder pain, nausea, faintness, dizziness or loss of consciousness, or heavy bleeding, is also an emergency. In someone with cirrhosis, vomiting blood, very dark/black stools or sudden confusion/slurred speech need emergency care. These are alternative triggers, not an all-signs checklist. The affected person must not drive; arrange another driver or an ambulance.

A newborn’s symptoms do not replace the prevention plan

An exposed baby may have no early signs of infection, so keep vaccination and testing appointments. Seek immediate emergency assessment for breathing difficulty or very fast breathing, blue/grey or unusually pale/blotchy colour, cold or damp skin, difficulty waking or loss of consciousness, a seizure, a weak, high-pitched or continuous cry, an abnormal response, not feeding, unusual sleepiness or no urine for 12 hours. A temperature of 38°C or more under three months, below 36°C or shivering also needs immediate emergency assessment.

Jaundice in the first 24 hours is an emergency. In a baby, jaundice with unusual sleepiness or difficult waking, not feeding, floppiness, stiffness or jerking, temperature of 38°C or more or 36°C or less, abnormal hot/cold feeling or shivering, no wet nappies or breathing difficulty also needs emergency assessment. Later new or worsening jaundice, dark urine or pale stools needs urgent clinical advice. Do not wait for every sign or the hepatitis test. Ask another adult to drive or arrange an ambulance rather than driving while caring for an acutely unwell baby.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask which virus and which test result establish the diagnosis, how liver health and other infections affect the plan, and whether exposure requires time-sensitive prevention. Bring prior treatment and vaccine records.

Before birth, confirm who will arrange the baby’s hepatitis B vaccine, whether immunoglobulin is indicated, the local timing and the later vaccine and blood-test appointments. Maternal treatment is not a substitute.

Keep separate follow-up plans for parent and baby, discuss exact medicines and feeding, and seek urgent help for changing symptoms rather than waiting to finish records or reach a routine appointment.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organize appointments, virus and test names, prescribed medicines, vaccine dates, the baby’s written prevention plan and questions for maternity, liver and child-care teams. It cannot diagnose hepatitis, interpret viral loads, calculate a personal loss or transmission risk, choose medicines or immunoglobulin, or replace urgent care. Use records to support the clinical plan, not delay it.

When to seek help

Seek urgent advice for suspected hepatitis or new jaundice. Pregnancy bleeding or pelvic pain needs prompt assessment; reduced or changed usual fetal movements needs immediate maternity contact. Emergency help is needed for severe/worsening/movement- or touch-provoked pelvic pain, or pelvic pain with faintness/dizziness/passing out, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or sudden confusion. Pregnancy bleeding with severe abdominal pain, shoulder pain, nausea, faintness/dizziness/loss of consciousness, or heavy bleeding, is also an emergency. Known cirrhosis with vomiting blood, black stools or sudden confusion/slurred speech is an emergency. The affected person must not drive. A baby with breathing difficulty, abnormal blue/grey/pale/blotchy colour, cold or damp skin, difficulty waking or loss of consciousness, seizure, a weak/high-pitched/continuous cry, abnormal response, not feeding, unusual sleepiness or no urine for 12 hours needs emergency assessment; so does 38°C or more under three months, below 36°C or shivering. Jaundice before 24 hours, or with unusual sleepiness/difficult waking, not feeding, floppy/stiff/jerking movements, 38°C or more or 36°C or less, abnormal hot/cold feeling or shivering, no wet nappies or breathing difficulty is also an emergency. Later new/worsening jaundice, dark urine or pale stools needs urgent advice. These are alternatives, not an all-signs checklist. Arrange another driver or an ambulance rather than driving while caring for an acutely unwell baby.

Evidence notes updated: November 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A–E are different infections. Pregnancy-loss risk and care depend on the virus, acute or chronic illness, liver health and the individual situation.
  • HBV-exposed newborn prevention must be planned before birth; maternal antivirals do not replace vaccine and any indicated immunoglobulin.
  • Complete the local infant vaccine and testing pathway even when the baby looks well. US and England schedules are not interchangeable.
  • HCV has no vaccine; current infection and infant follow-up matter. D depends on B, and E needs particular pregnancy vigilance.
  • Possible exposure, jaundice, maternal illness or a baby’s emergency warning signs should not wait for a routine appointment.

Frequently asked questions

Which hepatitis viruses can pass from a pregnant person to a baby?

B and C are important perinatal infections. D can rarely pass around birth in the context of B, and E can also pass to a baby. The route and risk depend on the virus and infection status; a parent’s positive result does not prove that the baby is infected. For HBV, agree birth vaccination and immunoglobulin eligibility in advance, then complete the local vaccine and test plan.

Can hepatitis C pass to the baby?

Yes, when the pregnant person has current infection with detectable HCV RNA. CDC estimates about 6–7% among perinatally exposed infants, with higher risk in poorly controlled HIV coinfection. There is no HCV vaccine and no caesarean or routine birth medicine guaranteed to prevent transmission. Arrange the baby’s age-appropriate test even if well.

Can hepatitis harm the pregnancy or cause a miscarriage?

The answer is not the same for every virus or every illness. A hepatitis diagnosis alone does not predict or explain a loss, but blanket reassurance is unsafe. Hepatitis E can cause severe maternal illness and fetal loss, particularly later in pregnancy. HCV has associations with preterm birth and growth problems, and cirrhosis increases risk. Ask the team to assess the type, liver health and pregnancy rather than applying a fixed percentage.

What should I do if I think I have hepatitis?

Contact a clinician urgently, particularly for jaundice, dark urine, pale stools or illness after possible exposure, and say you are pregnant or recently gave birth. Do not wait for all symptoms, try a liver detox or stop prescribed medicines yourself. Pregnancy pain or bleeding has its own urgent pathways; emergency alternatives are set out above.

Does every exposed baby get the same hepatitis B injections?

No single worldwide schedule applies. In the US, an infant of an HBsAg-positive person receives hepatitis B vaccine and HBIG within 12 hours, then completes the course and has the planned blood tests. England uses birth vaccine within 24 hours and HBIG for selected higher-risk infants. Unknown maternal status and low birth weight require the birth team’s urgent local protocol. Maternal treatment does not remove the need for newborn prevention.

Do A and E never become chronic, and is there a vaccine for every type?

A does not become chronic; E is usually acute but rarely persists, particularly with immunosuppression. A and B vaccines are available, B vaccination also prevents D infection in someone not already infected, and there is no HCV vaccine. An HEV vaccine exists in limited settings, including outbreak programmes, but is not universally available or routinely recommended for every pregnancy.

Can I breastfeed with hepatitis B or C?

HBV does not automatically prevent breastfeeding when the baby receives appropriate birth prophylaxis. HCV is not documented to spread in milk, but cracked, damaged or bleeding nipples need a temporary feeding plan to prevent blood exposure. HIV coinfection and the exact medicines require separate advice. Ordinary hugging and kissing do not transmit HCV.

Which symptoms should not wait for a hepatitis appointment?

Severe, worsening or movement/touch-provoked pelvic pain, or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, passing out, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or sudden confusion needs emergency help. Pregnancy bleeding with severe abdominal pain, shoulder pain, nausea, faintness, dizziness or loss of consciousness, or heavy bleeding, is another emergency. Known cirrhosis with vomiting blood, black stools or sudden confusion/slurred speech also needs emergency care; do not self-drive. A baby with breathing difficulty, abnormal blue/grey/pale/blotchy colour, cold or damp skin, difficulty waking or loss of consciousness, seizure, a weak/high-pitched/continuous cry, abnormal response, not feeding, unusual sleepiness or no urine for 12 hours needs emergency assessment; so does 38°C or more under three months, below 36°C or shivering. Jaundice before 24 hours, or with unusual sleepiness, difficult waking, not feeding, floppy/stiff/jerking movements, 38°C or more or 36°C or less, abnormal hot/cold feeling or shivering, no wet nappies or breathing difficulty is also an emergency. Later new/worsening jaundice, dark urine or pale stools needs urgent advice. These are alternatives; do not wait for all signs. Arrange another driver or an ambulance rather than driving while caring for an acutely unwell baby.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
